description: I like to find correlation in patterns of data.
summary:
Earth Systems Trend Detective is an interactive, reproducible Python platform for discovering and measuring environmental trends worldwide. It combines NASA MERRA-2 and GPM precipitation data with USGS earthquake records, Smithsonian volcanic histories, and tectonic plate models. Across 2,592 global grid cells and 21 years (2005–2025), users can explore maps and time series, estimate rates of change, and assess statistical significance using confidence intervals and Mann–Kendall tests.

We extended NASA's trend-detection challenge by testing whether rapid temperature changes, hydrological conditions, volcanic activity, and tectonic information improve 3- and 7-day earthquake forecasts. Two XGBoost models—a seismicity/tectonics baseline and an integrated Earth-system model—were evaluated on held-out observations. We found significant temperature trends in 280 grid cells, but the added variables did not improve forecasting accuracy. The project makes complex Earth-system data explorable while demonstrating the value of transparent, reproducible negative results.
details:
The project provides a Jupyter-based global trend explorer and a reproducible earthquake-forecasting experiment. Users inspect interactive geographic maps, select environmental variables and time periods, view time series, quantify trends in scientific units, and examine confidence intervals and corrected significance results.

Our pipeline harmonizes NASA MERRA-2 atmospheric/land variables and GPM IMERG precipitation with USGS seismicity, Smithsonian eruption history, and global plate-boundary and motion models. It processes 2005–2025 observations into 2,592 worldwide 5° cells, engineering temperature-reversal, hydrological, volcanic, and tectonic features. GPU-accelerated XGBoost compares an integrated model against a seismicity/tectonics baseline for 3- and 7-day forecasts.

Built with Python, Jupyter, Pandas, Xarray, geospatial/statistical libraries, Plotly, and an NVIDIA Titan RTX, the tool makes Earth-science change accessible and testable. Its novelty is linking interactive trend discovery to a falsifiable forecasting hypothesis. Design priorities included global coverage, missing-data transparency, limited resources, data-release timing, leakage prevention, and rigorous holdout evaluation. Results showed significant environmental trends, but no predictive benefit from the additional inputs.
